title: Jensen Huang’s affair exposes Silicon Valley’s national security power
gist: Alpert argues the 8 November 2026 revelation that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman US intelligence reportedly assesses as a Chinese MSS asset exposes how tech executives now wield national-security power that counterintelligence is not built to protect — and that Trump, briefed months earlier, chose politically to keep and defend Huang.

insights.claim: On 8 November 2026 Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an affair, and according to the New York Times US intelligence agencies concluded his mistress is an asset of China's Ministry of State Security.
insights.speaker: Cory Alpert
insights.so_what: Key-person and governance risk for NVDA; potential regulatory scrutiny of China chip-sales policy.

insights.claim: News of the affair shocked markets and regulators given Nvidia's status as the world's most valuable company and its centrality to Western tech competition with China.
insights.speaker: Cory Alpert
insights.so_what: Headline volatility in NVDA and AI-complex; watch for board/governance responses.
insights.quote: News of the affair shocked markets and regulators.

insights.claim: The threat against Huang centred on potential Chinese influence over Nvidia's position on selling AI chips to China, rather than theft of classified information.
insights.speaker: Cory Alpert
insights.so_what: Raises political scrutiny of Nvidia's China export lobbying; could harden export-control stance.
insights.quote: The threat against Huang centred on the potential for China to influence Nvidia’s position on selling AI chips to China

insights.claim: Trump was briefed on Huang's relationship and the intelligence assessment well before the public, yet continued speaking with Huang and publicly defended him after the scandal broke — a political decision because Trump saw Huang as indispensable.
insights.speaker: Cory Alpert
insights.so_what: Suggests Huang's political protection remains intact under Trump; reduces near-term risk of forced exit.
insights.quote: The decision to do nothing with the information developed by the FBI was a political one

themes.theme: Tech executives as structural national-security actors

insights.claim: Nvidia controls 80–85% of the global AI chip hardware market, positioning itself at the vanguard of American power through infrastructure control; Huang told CSIS in December 2025 that 'our nation's extraordinary technology industry is part of our national security'.
insights.speaker: Cory Alpert
insights.so_what: Nvidia's near-monopoly makes it a geopolitical asset and target — policy risk is structural.

insights.claim: In September 2026 the Pentagon named Elon Musk, Anduril founder Palmer Luckey and Newt Gingrich to lead Project Meridian, guiding future US warfare including acquisition of hundreds of billions of dollars of equipment.
insights.speaker: Cory Alpert
insights.so_what: Defence-tech firms tied to these executives (SpaceX, Anduril) positioned for large procurement flows.

insights.claim: Silicon Valley executives are giving themselves the job of shaping US national-security interests rather than delivering what government requests, making them structurally decisive figures in policy.
insights.speaker: Cory Alpert
insights.so_what: Corporate decisions by tech leaders are now geopolitical events to monitor.
insights.quote: The leaders of major American technology firms are becoming structurally decisive figures in American national security policy.

insights.claim: Musk's throttling of Starlink access for Ukrainian soldiers raised the question of whether Musk or Trump authorised it, showing critical decisions can be made on either side of the public–private wall.
insights.speaker: Cory Alpert
insights.so_what: Private control of military-critical infrastructure is a sovereign-risk factor for allies relying on US tech.

insights.claim: During Brazil's presidential election, Lula's campaign alleged Meta's platforms promoted his opponent and limited his reach, prompting protests at Meta's São Paulo office; a majority of Brazilians now believe American technology poses a national-security risk.
insights.speaker: Cory Alpert
insights.so_what: Rising foreign backlash raises regulatory/sovereignty risk for US platforms abroad.
insights.quote: a majority of Brazilians believe that American technology poses a risk to their national security

insights.claim: US counterintelligence (FBI) is designed to protect classified information and hardware from theft, but executives who control technology used by militaries can make consequential decisions without classified access, requiring counterintelligence to be reimagined.
insights.speaker: Cory Alpert
insights.so_what: Expect future policy proposals on counterintelligence vetting of tech executives.

insights.claim: Even adapted counterintelligence services can be countermanded by chief executives making political calculations, as Huang's MAGA embrace helped Trump build Silicon Valley support.
insights.speaker: Cory Alpert
insights.so_what: Political alignment, not institutions, currently determines tech-executive accountability.

insights.claim: Backlash against Silicon Valley's accumulated power was part of voters' midterm rebuke, and new leaders from both parties will have to reimagine national security to cover private actors' public power.
insights.speaker: Cory Alpert
insights.so_what: Post-midterm Congress may push tech oversight and AI/chip governance legislation — regulatory overhang for megacap tech.

insights.claim: These vulnerabilities will not stop at US borders, affecting every country that relies on American technology in civilian and public sectors.
insights.speaker: Cory Alpert
insights.so_what: Supports 'sovereign tech' demand abroad (sovereign AI, local cloud).
